items.title: Beyond blood: a narrative review of advancements in saliva-based diagnostics.
items.summary: This narrative review examined the potential of human saliva as a noninvasive diagnostic biofluid capable of replacing or supplementing conventional blood-based testing. The authors synthesized current evidence on salivary biomarkers spanning glycemic control, cardiovascular risk, sepsis surveillance, endocrinology, infectious diseases, oncological liquid biopsy, and neurodegenerative disorders, while also evaluating analytical technologies from immunoassays and mass spectrometry to wearable electrochemical biosensors. The review further distinguished between regulatory-cleared diagnostic platforms and those still in discovery phases. Despite promising advances, the authors found that widespread clinical adoption is hindered by unstandardized collection protocols, oral matrix interference, and the absence of validated normative reference intervals. They conclude that translation into mainstream diagnostics will require universal sampling standardization, matrix-matched biosensor engineering for sub-picomolar detection, and rigorous multicenter prospective trials to establish clinical cutoffs and validate blood-saliva correlation kinetics.
items.citation: Mondal S, Das Sharma A, Mandal SK et al.. Beyond blood: a narrative review of advancements in saliva-based diagnostics.. Expert review of molecular diagnostics. 2026

items.title: Consented Universal Newborn Screening for Congenital Cytomegalovirus Infection Using Dried Blood Spot and Dried Saliva Spot Specimens: Implementation and Relative Programmatic Accuracy.
items.summary: This study evaluated two specimen types for universal newborn screening of congenital cytomegalovirus infection, comparing dried blood spots and dried saliva spots collected at birth across multiple centers using quantitative PCR assays. The prospective pilot enrolled consecutive births and offered confirmatory urine testing to any newborn who screened positive on either specimen type. Dried saliva spots did not significantly improve sensitivity for detecting congenital cytomegalovirus infection compared to dried blood spots, while producing a substantially higher false positive rate, with each additional true case identified by saliva but missed by blood associated with multiple additional false positives. Saliva-based screening also extended turnaround times, frequently failing to return results within the window needed to offer a definitively diagnostic confirmatory test for congenital infection. Based on this performance profile, the authors concluded that dried saliva spot screening did not support population-wide implementation within their program.
items.citation: Santander E, Reuvers E, Lacaria M et al.. Consented Universal Newborn Screening for Congenital Cytomegalovirus Infection Using Dried Blood Spot and Dried Saliva Spot Specimens: Implementation and Relative Programmatic Accuracy.. International journal of neonatal screening. 2026

items.title: Vitamin D<sub>3</sub> oral rinsing reduces salivary SARS-CoV-2 antigen detectability: a clinical trial with public health implications.
items.summary: This clinical trial investigated whether rinsing the mouth with a Vitamin D₃ solution could affect the accuracy of saliva-based rapid antigen tests for SARS-CoV-2. Researchers enrolled adults with confirmed SARS-CoV-2 infection and collected paired saliva samples immediately before and after a standardized one-minute Vitamin D₃ oral rinse, analyzing each sample with both rapid antigen testing and rapid RT-PCR under blinded conditions. The rinse converted a large majority of rapid antigen test results from positive to negative, substantially reducing antigen detectability, while RT-PCR positivity and viral RNA levels remained largely unchanged between the paired samples. These discordant findings indicate that the oral rinse interfered with antigen detection without eliminating the underlying viral RNA, pointing to a pre-analytical variable that can produce false-negative rapid antigen test results. The authors conclude that Vitamin D₃ oral rinsing represents a previously underappreciated factor that could compromise saliva-based infectious disease screening and public health surveillance.
items.citation: Feteih SMN, Heaphy ELG, Aljagthmi A et al.. Vitamin D<sub>3</sub> oral rinsing reduces salivary SARS-CoV-2 antigen detectability: a clinical trial with public health implications.. Frontiers in oral health. 2026

items.title: Sample-to-answer automated centrifugal microfluidics with computer-vision readout for point-of-care molecular diagnostics
items.summary: This paper addressed the need for decentralized, automated molecular diagnostics highlighted by the COVID-19 pandemic, particularly for settings where centralized laboratory infrastructure is limited or overwhelmed. The researchers developed a fully automated centrifugal microfluidic platform that integrates loop-mediated isothermal amplification with computer-vision-based optical readout, performing the entire assay from sample to answer at the press of a single button without user intervention. The system was demonstrated using SARS-CoV-2 detection as a model application, processing multiple samples in a single run within roughly forty minutes. Testing with RNA fragments spiked into water and artificial saliva showed consistent detection down to a low copy-number sensitivity per reaction. The authors propose that this platform architecture is broadly generalizable to other infectious disease targets and represents a practical template for rapid, point-of-care molecular diagnostics in future outbreak scenarios.
items.citation: Akhtar AS, Lapins N, Moura JM et al.. Sample-to-answer automated centrifugal microfluidics with computer-vision readout for point-of-care molecular diagnostics. 2026

items.title: Diagnostic Accuracy of Molecular Testing on Saliva and Oral Swabs for Pulmonary Tuberculosis.
items.summary: This study evaluated the diagnostic accuracy of molecular testing on saliva and oral swabs as non-sputum alternatives for detecting pulmonary tuberculosis, addressing a critical gap in TB diagnostics. Using a nested case-control design within a prospective cohort of adults and children at primary care centers in Colombia, participants provided sputum for culture alongside saliva and nylon-flocked oral swab samples, which were tested using Xpert MTB/RIF Ultra. Saliva demonstrated high sensitivity and specificity against culture-confirmed TB, surpassing the World Health Organization's target threshold for non-sputum diagnostic tests, while oral swabs showed lower sensitivity but comparably high specificity. Saliva sensitivity significantly exceeded that of oral swabs, though the two methods did not differ significantly in specificity. Both sample types were well accepted by participants, supporting their potential as practical, non-sputum diagnostic approaches for pulmonary tuberculosis.
items.venue: Clinical infectious diseases : an official publication of the Infectious Diseases Society of America
items.citation: Vargas DA, Fuertes-Bucheli JF, Sanchez-Hidalgo A et al.. Diagnostic Accuracy of Molecular Testing on Saliva and Oral Swabs for Pulmonary Tuberculosis.. Clinical infectious diseases : an official publication of the Infectious Diseases Society of America. 2026

items.title: Altered immune response to exercise in patients with chronic fatigue syndrome/myalgic encephalomyelitis: A systematic literature review
items.summary: This paper systematically reviewed the scientific literature on how the immune system of patients with Chronic Fatigue Syndrome/myalgic encephalomyelitis responds to exercise compared to healthy sedentary controls. The researchers searched major databases and evaluated case-control studies for methodological quality before synthesizing their findings. They found that CFS patients exhibit a more pronounced activation of the complement system, enhanced oxidative stress with a delayed and reduced antioxidant response, and altered immune cell gene expression following exercise, though no differences were observed in circulating pro- or anti-inflammatory cytokines. Many of these immune alterations were found to relate to post-exertional malaise, a hallmark feature of the illness. Overall, the review concluded that there is level B evidence supporting an altered immune response to exercise in CFS patients.
items.citation: Jo Nijs, Aandrea Nees, Lorna Paul et al.. Altered immune response to exercise in patients with chronic fatigue syndrome/myalgic encephalomyelitis: A systematic literature review. Exercise immunology review. 2026

items.title: Andes virus outbreak linked to expedition cruise ship travel, multi-country investigation and response, April to June 2026
items.summary: The abstract describes an active outbreak investigation of Andes orthohantavirus linked to an expedition cruise ship, involving cases among passengers and crew from dozens of nationalities. Authorities conducted medical evacuations, repatriations, and coordinated international contact tracing, isolation, quarantine, and laboratory testing across multiple countries. The outbreak resulted in a substantial case fatality proportion, with cases identified among both passenger and crew populations. Investigations were ongoing at the time of reporting, with the source of the outbreak, specific risk factors, and transmission dynamics yet to be fully determined.
items.citation: Oda E. van den Berg, UKHSA ANDV Team, Ettore Severi et al.. Andes virus outbreak linked to expedition cruise ship travel, multi-country investigation and response, April to June 2026. Eurosurveillance. 2026

items.title: Advances and Challenges in Wearable Sensors for Health Monitoring
items.summary: This mega-review examines the current state of wearable sensor technologies for continuous and non-invasive health monitoring, bringing together researchers across the field to synthesize progress and identify outstanding challenges. The paper covers chemical biosensors operating across a range of biological fluids such as sweat, saliva, tears, interstitial fluid, and cerebrospinal fluid, alongside physical sensors for parameters including heart rate, blood pressure, and body temperature. Device formats reviewed span smart contact lenses, textiles, mouthguards, wristbands, and implantable systems, with dedicated attention to soft electronics, materials science advances, and strategies for energy harvesting and self-powering. The review also addresses signal acquisition and transmission, and discusses how artificial intelligence and machine learning can improve analytical performance and handle the large data volumes these devices generate. Beyond the technical landscape, the authors examine business, regulatory, and ethical considerations, framing the review as both a synthesis of the field and a guide for promising future research directions.
items.citation: Laís Canniatti Brazaca, Alvaro Moreno Lozano, Beatriz Mayol et al.. Advances and Challenges in Wearable Sensors for Health Monitoring. ACS Applied Materials & Interfaces. 2026

items.title: Hantavirus Emergence in a Changing World: Virology, Pathogenesis, Surveillance, and One Health Preparedness
items.summary: This review examines hantaviruses as emerging rodent-borne pathogens responsible for two serious clinical syndromes — hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome and hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome — that together represent a growing global public health concern. The authors synthesize current knowledge spanning virology, epidemiology, pathogenesis, clinical presentation, diagnostics, and surveillance, with particular attention to how climate change, urbanization, and land-use transformation drive shifts in rodent reservoir populations and increase spillover risk to humans. The review identifies significant surveillance and diagnostic gaps in tropical and Caribbean regions where hantavirus circulation is likely underrecognized. Advances discussed include molecular and genomic diagnostic tools, vaccine candidates, monoclonal antibody therapies, and climate-informed early warning systems. The authors argue that integrated One Health frameworks combining human, animal, and environmental monitoring — alongside strengthened laboratory capacity and regional collaboration — are essential for improving outbreak preparedness and reducing the global disease burden of hantavirus infections.
items.citation: Maria E. Ramos‐Niño, Nicolette Chiem, Prakash V. A. K. Ramdass. Hantavirus Emergence in a Changing World: Virology, Pathogenesis, Surveillance, and One Health Preparedness. Microorganisms. 2026

items.title: Integrated microfluidic biosensors: shaping the future of quantitative life sciences and on-chip molecular diagnostics
items.summary: This review paper examines the integration of microfluidic technologies with biosensing platforms and their applications across the life sciences and medical diagnostics. The authors survey a broad range of microfluidic approaches, including three-dimensional cell culture systems, inertial separation, acoustofluidics, dielectrophoresis, optofluidics, and immunoassays, alongside biosensor modalities such as electrochemical, electrophysiological, plasmonic, Raman, and quantum sensing. These combined systems are capable of detecting analytes spanning a wide size range, from nanometer-scale nucleic acids and proteins to millimeter-scale organisms, and find application in human and animal health, environmental monitoring, and point-of-care diagnostics. The review argues that the synergy between microfluidics and biosensing confers advantages in sensitivity, speed, portability, and real-time monitoring that neither field achieves alone. The authors also address existing technical challenges, future development opportunities, and highlight commercial products that have successfully emerged from integrated microfluidic technologies.
items.citation: Ty Downing Naquin, Chloe M. Naquin, Qian WU et al.. Integrated microfluidic biosensors: shaping the future of quantitative life sciences and on-chip molecular diagnostics. Lab on a Chip. 2026

items.title: Evolving Approaches to Bacterial Identification: A Review of Classical and Modern Techniques
items.summary: This review examines the full spectrum of bacterial identification methods, motivated by the ongoing global burden of infectious diseases and rising antimicrobial resistance. The authors surveyed classical techniques such as microscopy, culture, biochemical testing, and immunological assays alongside advanced approaches including mass spectrometry, various forms of polymerase chain reaction, whole-genome sequencing, metagenomics, and artificial intelligence-enhanced analysis. Emerging technologies such as CRISPR-based diagnostics and phage- and nanomaterial-based detection systems are also discussed as promising alternatives to established methods. The review concludes that integrating these complementary approaches can improve the accuracy and speed of bacterial identification across clinical, veterinary, agricultural, and environmental contexts, but notes that conventional methods are constrained by slow turnaround times, reduced sensitivity, and difficulty detecting fastidious or uncultivable organisms. The authors emphasize that technological advancement must be accompanied by rigorous standardization, particularly in bioinformatics frameworks, where variability in algorithm-defined thresholds currently limits the routine implementation of whole-genome sequencing.
items.citation: Ina Gajić, Milos Jovicevic, Dušan Kekić et al.. Evolving Approaches to Bacterial Identification: A Review of Classical and Modern Techniques. International Journal of Molecular Sciences. 2026

In this framework the inflaton is a Wilson line, and a monodromy potential becomes available for large numbers of sites. Taking the continuum limit transforms the system so that the inflaton velocity corresponds to a five-dimensional electric field and the resulting friction becomes Ohmic dissipation, a mechanism the authors argue can sustain warm inflation in a manner consistent with observations.
items.citation: Anish Ghoshal, Alessandro Strumia. Ohmic warm inflation. arXiv. 2026

items.title: Is Neutrino Disappearance Sensitive to T-Violation for Asymmetric Matter Profiles ?
items.summary: The paper investigates whether T-violation can appear in neutrino disappearance channels, challenging the widely accepted claim that it cannot. The authors demonstrate that this conventional assertion holds only for symmetric matter profiles or when the Jarlskog invariant vanishes, and that the muon and tau neutrino survival probabilities contain a genuine sine-delta-dependent T-asymmetric term when matter profiles are asymmetric. They identify the source of the confusion as an improperly constructed T test that mathematically subtracts a probability from itself, and they carefully distinguish proper from improper T, CP, and CPT tests for arbitrary matter profiles. Using a two-layer constant-density toy model, they find that T-violation is maximized when one layer is near the solar resonance and the other near the atmospheric resonance. The paper also assesses whether the matter asymmetry encountered by current long-baseline experiments is sufficient to make this effect observable in muon neutrino survival probability, and discusses future experimental scenarios where such T and CP violation could be probed in disappearance channels.
items.citation: Gabriela Barenboim, Stephen J. Parke, Alberto Sánchez Vargas. Is Neutrino Disappearance Sensitive to T-Violation for Asymmetric Matter Profiles ?. arXiv. 2026

items.title: Optimal Linear Regression Without a Variance
items.summary: This paper studies linear regression in the challenging "infinite variance" regime, where the noise distribution has only a finite moment of order strictly between one and two, and the covariates may also have limited moment conditions. The authors develop a black-box reduction that transforms any finite-variance linear regression procedure into one that handles these heavy-tailed, weak-moment settings, using a technique called empirical residual pruning that requires no knowledge of the moment exponent, noise scale, or covariance structure. Under a finite fourth-moment condition on the covariates, their approach achieves high-probability error bounds that match the minimax-optimal rate for this regime, scaling as the sample size raised to the power determined by the moment exponent. They prove a matching minimax lower bound confirming the optimality of these rates and show that the reduction preserves computational efficiency relative to the finite-variance subroutine it wraps. Extensions include a distribution-free prediction guarantee under bounded raw moment assumptions and an analogous moment-agnostic reduction for the simpler problem of mean estimation.

items.title: No Polynomial-Time Algorithm For Tarski Fixed Points Unless Cryptographic Assumptions Fail

The authors construct a subexponential-time reduction from the Unique End of Potential Line problem to the Tarski fixed point problem, thereby transferring known cryptographic hardness results for the former to the latter. This yields conditional lower bounds on the running time of any algorithm finding a Tarski fixed point, with the strongest results establishing quasi-polynomial-time lower bounds under standard cryptographic assumptions, as well as under a weak exponential-time hypothesis for the source problem. Notably, these time complexity lower bounds align with recently established quasi-polynomial query complexity lower bounds for the same problem, suggesting that quasi-polynomial time may be essentially optimal for this problem unless foundational cryptographic assumptions fail.

items.title: Hölder continuity of meromorphic functions and equisingularity
items.summary: This paper investigates meromorphic functions on complex analytic varieties that satisfy Hölder continuity conditions with respect to the outer metric, organizing them into sheaves parameterized by a Hölder exponent between zero and one. These sheaves interpolate between the structure sheaves of the seminormalization and the Lipschitz saturation, and the paper proves they are coherent with only finitely many distinct members, the transitional exponents being rational numbers determined by Rees valuations of a diagonal ideal. For reduced curve germs, the Hölder saturations are computed explicitly from the characteristic exponents of branches, and smoothness criteria are established, including the sharp threshold that a variety whose Hölder saturation is smooth for some exponent greater than one third must itself be smooth. The paper further shows that homeomorphic curves are bi-Hölder homeomorphic for some positive exponent, while bi-Hölder homeomorphisms with exponent sufficiently close to one preserve multiplicity. Building on these foundations, the authors introduce relative Hölder saturation for families of varieties and define two notions of equisingularity—Hölder equisingularity and the stronger Hölder equisaturation—showing that for families of reduced curve germs these notions interpolate between topological, Whitney, and Lipschitz equisingularity at explicit exponents depending on invariants of the special fiber.

items.title: MemOnce: A Scalable Memory Architecture for Large Language Models
items.summary: This paper addresses the challenge of efficiently maintaining memory states for large language models during long-horizon and continual interactions. The authors introduce MemOnce, a foundation architecture built around two key innovations: a memory encoder-decoder that caches a small subset of final-layer hidden states and dynamically reconstructs key-value caches for attention layers, and a memory sparse attention mechanism that adaptively retrieves relevant memory representations with sparse indices computed once across all layers. Together, these designs achieve linear-time complexity and dramatically reduce GPU memory footprint compared to standard Transformers, which suffer from linear memory growth and quadratic computational complexity as context expands. Through extensive experiments across varying model sizes, context lengths, and training paradigms, MemOnce is shown to outperform standard Transformers and other architectures, yielding substantial reductions in memory state cache size, prefill latency, and improvements in throughput and overall memory performance at very long contexts. The architecture also demonstrates zero-shot generalization to downstream representation tasks, achieving competitive results against specialized models.
items.citation: Chang Nie, Chaoyou Fu, Songlin Liu et al.. MemOnce: A Scalable Memory Architecture for Large Language Models. arXiv. 2026

items.title: Antimicrobial-laden PerOssal beads display in vitro inhibition and killing of extensively drug-resistant Gram-negative bacteria associated with conflict wounds in Ukraine
items.summary: This study investigated whether antimicrobial-laden PerOssal hydroxyapatite and calcium sulphate beads could inhibit and kill extensively drug-resistant Gram-negative bacteria isolated from conflict wounds in Ukraine, where high-energy open fractures, contamination, and delays to surgical care drive high infection rates. The researchers tested beads loaded with various antimicrobials—including gentamicin, tobramycin, cefazolin, co-amoxiclav, and a gentamicin-rifampicin combination—using zone-of-inhibition testing and time-kill analysis against bacterial isolates that were resistant to multiple standard systemic agents. Single-agent beads loaded with gentamicin, tobramycin, or cefazolin showed only weak inhibitory activity against these resistant isolates, but the gentamicin-rifampicin combination achieved consistent broad-spectrum inhibition and killing, and co-amoxiclav-loaded beads inhibited growth across all tested strains. The authors conclude that local antimicrobial delivery via these beads represents a promising strategy to reduce infection risk in heavily contaminated open fractures, particularly when timely surgical wound excision is not possible, with potential applications in both conflict and civilian disaster settings. They note that in vivo studies are needed to confirm the clinical effectiveness of this approach.
items.citation: Henry Adam Claireaux, Edward J. A. Douglas, Scott J C Pallett et al.. Antimicrobial-laden PerOssal beads display in vitro inhibition and killing of extensively drug-resistant Gram-negative bacteria associated with conflict wounds in Ukraine. Bone and Joint Research. 2026

items.title: Development and Application of a Dual-Readout RPA-PfAgo System for Rapid Detection of Streptococcus agalactiae in Bovine Milk
items.summary: This study developed and validated a molecular detection platform for *Streptococcus agalactiae*, a major cause of bovine mastitis, by combining recombinase polymerase amplification with the prokaryotic Argonaute protein from *Pyrococcus furiosus* (PfAgo) targeting the conserved *cfb* gene. The researchers screened multiple primer and guide DNA combinations to optimize the system, which was configured in two readout formats: a real-time fluorescence assay and a lateral flow dipstick assay. The fluorescence format achieved a lower detection limit than the dipstick format, and both demonstrated high analytical specificity with no cross-reactivity against non-target bacteria. Field validation using bovine milk samples from multiple dairy-farming regions in China showed that both RPA-PfAgo formats identified substantially more positive samples than traditional bacteriological culture, while achieving complete concordance with a standardized quantitative PCR assay across all samples tested. The authors conclude that this dual-readout platform offers a rapid, sensitive, and reliable diagnostic tool suitable for on-site detection of *S. agalactiae* in dairy settings.
items.citation: Xujie Zhao, Yuying Du, Qianlei Zhu et al.. Development and Application of a Dual-Readout RPA-PfAgo System for Rapid Detection of Streptococcus agalactiae in Bovine Milk. Veterinary Sciences. 2026

items.title: Modulation of Gut Microbiota Through Functional Foods to Reduce Low-Grade Chronic Inflammation
items.summary: This paper examined the relationship between gut microbiota dysbiosis and chronic low-grade inflammation, which underlies conditions such as obesity, cardiovascular disease, metabolic syndrome, and cancer. The authors reviewed how the complex microbial community of the gastrointestinal tract regulates immune responses, nutrient metabolism, pathogen defense, and intestinal barrier integrity, and how disruptions to this community drive inflammatory and metabolic dysfunction. The paper assessed dietary interventions using functional foods — specifically probiotics, prebiotics, and bioactive compounds — as strategies to restore microbial balance by promoting beneficial bacteria and suppressing harmful microbial activity. The authors also highlighted how advances in microbiome sequencing technologies have deepened understanding of host–microbe interactions, enabling more targeted nutritional approaches. Overall, the paper concludes that modulating the gut microbiota through functional foods represents a promising non-invasive strategy for reducing chronic inflammation and improving metabolic and immune health.
authors: Pakistan Journal of Medical & Cardiological Review
items.venue: Pakistan Journal of Medical & Cardiological Review
items.citation: Pakistan Journal of Medical & Cardiological Review. Modulation of Gut Microbiota Through Functional Foods to Reduce Low-Grade Chronic Inflammation. Pakistan Journal of Medical & Cardiological Review. 2026

items.title: ECCO Guidelines on the Prevention, Diagnosis, and Management of Infections in Inflammatory Bowel Disease
items.summary: This paper presents updated clinical guidelines from a major European gastroenterology organization on the prevention, diagnosis, and management of infections in patients with inflammatory bowel disease. The guidelines were developed in response to the rapid expansion of immunosuppressive and biologic therapies used to treat Crohn's disease and ulcerative colitis, including newer small molecules and advanced biologics, each carrying distinct infection risk profiles. The document addresses opportunistic and other clinically significant infections across viral, bacterial, mycobacterial, and vaccine-preventable categories, with an emphasis on risk stratification tailored to contemporary treatment regimens. The update supersedes previous iterations of these consensus guidelines and integrates the most recent evidence to provide clinicians with a structured, evidence-based framework for minimizing infection-related morbidity and mortality in an increasingly immunocompromised patient population.
items.venue: Journal of Crohn s and Colitis
items.citation: Henit A. Yanai, Pierre Ellul, Bram Verstockt et al.. ECCO Guidelines on the Prevention, Diagnosis, and Management of Infections in Inflammatory Bowel Disease. Journal of Crohn s and Colitis. 2026

items.title: Gut Microbial Metabotypes Shape Polyphenol Bioactivity: Toward Precision Nutrition Strategies for Human Health
items.summary: This review paper examined how gut microbiota transform dietary polyphenols into bioactive metabolites and how individual differences in this capacity may influence the health effects of polyphenol-rich diets. Because many polyphenols are poorly absorbed in the upper gastrointestinal tract, they reach the colon where microbial communities convert them into distinct lower-molecular-weight metabolites such as urolithins, equol, and enterolignans, which can differ substantially in their biological activity compared to their parent compounds. The authors conducted a narrative review critically evaluating the concept of microbial metabotypes, which classify individuals by their capacity to produce specific microbial-derived metabolites, and assessed the evidence for associated biological effects spanning mitochondrial function, endothelial homeostasis, inflammation, and gut-brain communication. They found that while urolithin, equol, and enterolignan metabotypes represent relatively well-characterized models, the field is hampered by heterogeneous study protocols, non-standardized analytical thresholds, and insufficient validation across diverse populations. The authors conclude that microbial metabotypes currently hold promise as functional biomarkers for research and stratified trial design but are not yet sufficiently established to guide routine personalized dietary prescriptions.
items.citation: Pasquale Perrone, Stefania D’Angelo. Gut Microbial Metabotypes Shape Polyphenol Bioactivity: Toward Precision Nutrition Strategies for Human Health. Nutrients. 2026

items.title: Editor's Choice – European Society for Vascular Surgery (ESVS) 2026 Clinical Practice Guidelines on the Management of Vascular Graft and Endograft Infections
items.summary: These guidelines from the European Society for Vascular Surgery address the clinical management of vascular graft and endograft infections, updating a previous version to reflect current evidence and expert consensus. The document was developed by synthesizing and evaluating the best available scientific evidence, supplemented by expert opinion, with recommendations graded by both strength and level of evidence. A substantial set of recommendations was produced covering definitions, diagnosis, multidisciplinary team management, antimicrobial therapy, management of intracavitary and extracavitary infections, and follow-up. The guidelines also incorporate shared decision-making principles, including patient-facing information, and identify areas where evidence remains unresolved. The stated aim is to provide comprehensive, up-to-date guidance to assist clinicians and patients in selecting optimal management strategies for this serious condition.
items.venue: European Journal of Vascular and Endovascular Surgery
items.citation: Anne Lejay, Ben R. Saleem, Tara D. Barwick et al.. Editor's Choice – European Society for Vascular Surgery (ESVS) 2026 Clinical Practice Guidelines on the Management of Vascular Graft and Endograft Infections. European Journal of Vascular and Endovascular Surgery. 2026

items.title: Ohmic warm inflation
items.summary: The paper examines Warm Little Inflation, a previously proposed model of warm inflation in which dissipation maintains a thermal bath during the inflationary epoch, and identifies fundamental problems with it: the model is anomalous, lacks a viable inflaton potential, and cannot actually sustain the thermal bath because the quasi-static approximation used overestimates the dissipated power. To resolve these issues, the authors construct new anomaly-free models based on a fermion charged under a gauge group in an extra dimension, with a four-dimensional lattice formulation consisting of a ring of gauge groups with one fermion per site. In this construction the inflaton is a Wilson line, protected by gauge symmetry for sufficiently large numbers of sites, and a suitable monodromy potential emerges at large site number. Taking the continuum limit of the lattice theory maps the inflaton velocity to a five-dimensional electric field and the dissipation mechanism to Ohmic dissipation, which the authors argue can sustain warm inflation in a manner consistent with observational constraints.
items.citation: Anish Ghoshal, Alessandro Strumia. Ohmic warm inflation. arXiv. 2026

items.title: Is Neutrino Disappearance Sensitive to T-Violation for Asymmetric Matter Profiles ?
items.summary: The paper investigates whether neutrino disappearance channels can exhibit sensitivity to T-violation, challenging the widespread claim in the literature that T-violation is zero in such channels. The authors demonstrate that this claim holds only under restricted conditions — specifically for symmetric matter profiles or when the T/CP-violating phase causes the Jarlskog invariant to vanish — and that muon and tau neutrino survival probabilities carry a genuine sine-of-delta-dependent T asymmetry in asymmetric matter. They identify that the common misconception arises from applying an improper T test that amounts to subtracting a probability from itself rather than comparing physically distinct processes, and they carefully distinguish proper from improper T, CP, and CPT tests for general matter profiles. Using a two-layer constant-density toy model, they find that maximal T-violation occurs when one layer is near the solar resonance and the other near the atmospheric resonance. The paper further assesses whether the matter asymmetry encountered by long-baseline experiments is large enough to make the sine-of-delta dependence observable in muon neutrino survival probability, and discusses future experimental scenarios that could probe this effect.
items.citation: Gabriela Barenboim, Stephen J. Parke, Alberto Sánchez Vargas. Is Neutrino Disappearance Sensitive to T-Violation for Asymmetric Matter Profiles ?. arXiv. 2026

items.title: On the non-uniqueness of solutions of the axi-symmetric swirl-free Navier-Stokes equations, II
items.summary: This paper addresses the fundamental question of uniqueness for Leray solutions of the three-dimensional incompressible Navier-Stokes equations, focusing on the restricted class of axially symmetric swirl-free flows. The authors construct two distinct solutions sharing identical initial data that are smooth for all positive times, satisfy the energy identity, and belong to optimal Sobolev and critical Ladyzhenskaya-Prodi-Serrin function spaces — regularity classes in which uniqueness had long been expected to hold. Notably, this non-uniqueness is established within a symmetry class where smooth solutions are known to be globally regular, sharpening the paradox. The construction is computer-assisted and proceeds by rigorously verifying the existence of a linearly unstable forward self-similar solution, combining explicit asymptotic expansions with global residual estimates and weak coercivity inequalities stabilized by finitely many functionals. The instability of this self-similar profile, certified through quantitative inverse bounds and contraction arguments building on a companion paper, then generates the non-unique solutions.
items.citation: Matthieu Cadiot, Alexandru Ionescu, Hao Jia et al.. On the non-uniqueness of solutions of the axi-symmetric swirl-free Navier-Stokes equations, II. arXiv. 2026

items.title: Optimal Linear Regression Without a Variance
items.summary: This paper studies linear regression in the "infinite variance" regime, where the noise distribution has only a finite conditional moment of some unknown order strictly between one and two, and the covariates may also have only limited moment conditions. The authors develop a black-box reduction called empirical residual pruning that transforms any finite-variance linear regression procedure into one that handles these heavy-tailed, weak-moment settings, without requiring knowledge of the moment exponent, the noise scale, or the covariance structure. Under a finite fourth-moment condition on the covariates, any subroutine achieving the sub-Gaussian rate can be plugged into this reduction to yield high-probability error bounds that depend on the sample size, dimension, and confidence level in a natural way, and the reduction is computationally efficient whenever the subroutine is. The authors also establish a matching minimax lower bound under the same conditions, confirming that the achieved rates are optimal, and they extend the framework to distribution-free prediction guarantees and to mean estimation in analogous heavy-tailed settings.
items.citation: Artin Tajdini, Jasper C. H. Lee, Jonathan Scarlett et al.. Optimal Linear Regression Without a Variance. arXiv. 2026

items.title: Nearly pristine gas and hard ionizing radiation one billion years after the Big Bang
items.summary: This paper investigated the chemical and physical conditions of one of the earliest galaxies known, searching for evidence of the universe's first generation of stars (Population III stars), which are predicted to have formed from nearly metal-free primordial gas. Using deep spectroscopy from the James Webb Space Telescope, the researchers observed a strongly gravitationally magnified galaxy approximately one billion years after the Big Bang and measured its helium and hydrogen emission lines alongside its oxygen abundance. The galaxy shows helium emission at high significance, with helium-to-hydrogen line ratios consistent with extremely hard ionizing radiation fields and the low-metallicity conditions expected for Population III stellar populations. The oxygen abundance of the interstellar medium was found to be only a tiny fraction of the solar value, indicating a nearly pristine chemical environment that may have been enriched solely by Population III stars themselves. While alternative explanations such as accreting black holes cannot be ruled out, the findings demonstrate that pockets of near-primordial gas persisted well into the first billion years of cosmic history and were dominated by very massive stars.
items.citation: Takahiro Morishita, Massimo Stiavelli, Tommaso Treu et al.. Nearly pristine gas and hard ionizing radiation one billion years after the Big Bang. arXiv. 2026

items.title: No Polynomial-Time Algorithm For Tarski Fixed Points Unless Cryptographic Assumptions Fail
items.summary: The paper investigates the computational complexity of finding a fixed point of a monotone function on a lattice, known as a Tarski fixed point, whose existence is guaranteed by a classical theorem. The authors construct a subexponential-time reduction from the Unique End of Potential Line problem to the Tarski fixed point problem, thereby linking the difficulty of the latter to that of a well-studied computational problem with known cryptographic hardness. By applying established cryptographic lower bounds and a weak exponential-time hypothesis for the source problem, they derive conditional lower bounds on any algorithm that finds a Tarski fixed point, with the strongest results yielding quasi-polynomial-time lower bounds. These lower bounds are notable because they match recently established quasi-polynomial query complexity lower bounds for the same problem, suggesting that the query complexity essentially characterizes the computational difficulty.
items.citation: Eleni Batziou, John Fearnley, Alexandros Hollender et al.. No Polynomial-Time Algorithm For Tarski Fixed Points Unless Cryptographic Assumptions Fail. arXiv. 2026

items.title: Revisiting the use of adenosine deaminase in cerebrospinal fluid analysis for infectious meningoencephalitis.
items.summary: This study investigated the diagnostic utility of adenosine deaminase levels measured in cerebrospinal fluid across a range of central nervous system infections, with particular attention to tropical diseases and HIV-infected patients, populations in which this marker had been insufficiently studied. Researchers analyzed cerebrospinal fluid adenosine deaminase levels alongside other laboratory parameters in over two hundred patients with various microbiologically confirmed diagnoses, comparing results against a non-infectious control group and defining optimal diagnostic cutoff values. Significantly elevated cerebrospinal fluid adenosine deaminase levels were found in tuberculous meningitis and meningococcal meningitis compared to controls, with the marker showing modest sensitivity and specificity for these conditions and correlating positively with cerebrospinal fluid protein and negatively with cerebrospinal fluid glucose. Among patients with HIV coinfections, a significant difference in adenosine deaminase levels was observed only in those with varicella-zoster virus infection, and higher cutoff values were identified for central nervous system coinfections. The authors conclude that cerebrospinal fluid adenosine deaminase can serve as a supportive, though not standalone, diagnostic tool in suspected tuberculous meningitis, meningococcal meningitis, and central nervous system coinfections.
items.citation: Farias LABG, Neto OMV, Sobrinho EPL et al.. Revisiting the use of adenosine deaminase in cerebrospinal fluid analysis for infectious meningoencephalitis.. Arquivos de neuro-psiquiatria. 2026

items.title: Shotgun Metagenomics Versus 16S rDNA Sanger Sequencing for the Diagnosis of Blood Culture-Negative Endocarditis: A Draw?
items.summary: The paper investigated the diagnostic performance of two molecular methods — shotgun metagenomics and 16S rDNA Sanger sequencing — for identifying pathogens in blood culture-negative infective endocarditis. The researchers applied both techniques to the same DNA extracts obtained from surgically removed native valves, allowing a direct head-to-head comparison across cases classified as definite, possible, or rejected infective endocarditis. The two methods yielded comparable positivity rates overall, suggesting neither holds a clear advantage in terms of detecting an organism. However, metagenomics provided greater taxonomic resolution, meaning it could identify pathogens with more specificity when a signal was detected. The findings imply that while both approaches perform similarly in clinical sensitivity, metagenomics may offer an added benefit in characterizing the causative organism more precisely.
items.citation: Ben Brahim S, Royer G, Jacquier H et al.. Shotgun Metagenomics Versus 16S rDNA Sanger Sequencing for the Diagnosis of Blood Culture-Negative Endocarditis: A Draw?. Open forum infectious diseases. 2026

items.title: Case Report: Community-acquired pneumonia due to coinfection with <i>Streptococcus pneumoniae</i> and <i>Legionella pneumophila</i>.
items.summary: This case report describes a patient with severe community-acquired pneumonia caused by simultaneous infection with both *Streptococcus pneumoniae* and *Legionella pneumophila*, a co-infection that is rarely documented. The patient, a middle-aged man with several underlying comorbidities, presented with bilateral bronchopneumonia and pleural effusion, and was investigated using a combination of urinary antigen testing and molecular diagnostics to identify the causative pathogens. Diagnosis was confirmed by detecting *Legionella pneumophila* serogroup 1 via urinary antigen and *Streptococcus pneumoniae* via real-time PCR from sputum. The patient was treated with combined targeted antimicrobial therapy alongside supportive care, ultimately achieving complete recovery despite multiple complications during hospitalization. The authors argue that this case underscores the need to consider bacterial co-infection in severe pneumonia presentations and demonstrates the diagnostic value of pairing urinary antigen testing with molecular methods for timely, accurate pathogen identification.
items.citation: Petrusevska-Marinkovic S, Janeku Kartalova M, Aleksoski K et al.. Case Report: Community-acquired pneumonia due to coinfection with <i>Streptococcus pneumoniae</i> and <i>Legionella pneumophila</i>.. Frontiers in medicine. 2026

items.title: Bacterial Meningitis: A Review of Clinical and Public Health Testing.
items.summary: This review examined the major causative agents of bacterial meningitis and the testing approaches used to detect, characterize, and surveil these pathogens in both clinical and public health settings. The paper outlined the principal bacterial agents responsible for meningitis along with rarer causes, and described available diagnostic methods including Gram staining, culture, and molecular testing. A key finding highlighted is that culture-based detection can fail when antibiotic therapy is initiated early, making molecular approaches such as laboratory-developed PCR tests at public health laboratories increasingly important for pathogen detection and serotyping. Public health laboratories contribute additional capacity through antimicrobial susceptibility testing, serogroup determination, and whole genome sequencing, which collectively support outbreak investigations and vaccine development. The review concludes that integrating clinical and public health laboratory efforts provides comprehensive data to better characterize transmission, reduce disease burden, and improve vaccine strategies.
items.citation: Mitchell K, Musser KA. Bacterial Meningitis: A Review of Clinical and Public Health Testing.. Current clinical microbiology reports. 2026

items.title: Diagnostic Performance of the FilmArray BCID2 Multiplex PCR Panel Applied to Excised Heart Valve Specimens from Patients with Infective Endocarditis.
items.summary: This study investigated whether the FilmArray Blood Culture Identification 2 multiplex PCR panel could be applied off-label to excised heart valve tissue from patients with infective endocarditis to improve pathogen identification. Excised valve specimens from patients undergoing surgery for infective endocarditis were analyzed using the BCID2 panel, and the results were compared against conventional blood culture and valve culture methods. When benchmarked against blood culture, the BCID2 panel showed moderate sensitivity and a high positive predictive value, but agreement between the two methods was low overall. Compared with conventional valve culture, the BCID2 panel demonstrated very low sensitivity but perfect specificity. The authors conclude that the off-label use of this panel on valve tissue may serve as a complement to standard microbiological methods in selected patients, but a negative result cannot exclude infective endocarditis, and larger multicenter studies are needed to clarify its clinical utility.
items.citation: Bilewska A, Skrzeczyńska J, Dorota M et al.. Diagnostic Performance of the FilmArray BCID2 Multiplex PCR Panel Applied to Excised Heart Valve Specimens from Patients with Infective Endocarditis.. Microorganisms. 2026

items.title: Rapid identification of porcine bacterial pathogens using an artificial intelligence Raman microbial analyzer for biology.
items.summary: This study evaluated whether an AI-powered Raman spectroscopy platform could rapidly and accurately identify bacterial pathogens isolated from diseased pigs in a clinical veterinary diagnostic setting. The researchers collected bacterial isolates from multiple tissues of diseased pigs, confirmed species identity using polymerase chain reaction as a reference standard, and then assessed the system's ability to classify isolates across fourteen clinically relevant swine pathogens. The commercial system, which combines Raman spectroscopy with deep learning, delivered species-level identification in approximately two minutes per isolate without requiring labels or reagents. The system demonstrated high overall performance, achieving perfect recall for some of the most common pathogens such as *Pasteurella multocida* and *Salmonella enterica* serovar Choleraesuis, and recall exceeding ninety percent for other important species including *Escherichia coli*, *Streptococcus suis*, and *Glaesserella parasuis*. The authors conclude that this approach offers a rapid, automated, and cost-effective alternative to conventional diagnostic methods, with practical value for timely veterinary decision-making and relevance to public health given the zoonotic potential of several swine pathogens.
items.citation: Lu C-H, Ke N-J, Liu C-C et al.. Rapid identification of porcine bacterial pathogens using an artificial intelligence Raman microbial analyzer for biology.. Microbiology spectrum. 2026

items.title: Point-of-care testing in the diagnosis of infectious diseases.
items.summary: This review examined point-of-care testing as a diagnostic strategy for infectious diseases, motivated by the growing global burden of such diseases and the escalating threat of antimicrobial resistance. The authors surveyed the core technical platforms underlying current point-of-care technologies, including lateral flow assays, chemiluminescence immunoassays, isothermal amplification, CRISPR-based diagnostics, and microfluidic chip systems, as well as their application across a range of infection types spanning respiratory, bloodstream, gastrointestinal, urinary tract, and sexually transmitted infections. The review assessed both immunochromatographic and molecular diagnostic modalities, weighing their technical characteristics against practical clinical applicability. While acknowledging limitations in detection sensitivity, quality control, cost, and clinical integration, the authors conclude that advances in nanomaterials, microfluidic engineering, artificial intelligence, and industry standardization are driving improvements in performance and usability. On this basis, they argue that point-of-care testing is poised to become a central diagnostic tool for precision clinical management and public health epidemic control.
items.citation: Fang Q, Lin Y, Hu G et al.. Point-of-care testing in the diagnosis of infectious diseases.. Frontiers in microbiology. 2026

items.title: Finger-actuated microfluidic device for point-of-care circulating cell-free nucleic acid extraction.
items.summary: This paper developed a fully finger-actuated microfluidic device designed to extract cell-free nucleic acids from plasma at the point of care, without requiring external power sources or laboratory pipetting equipment. The device integrates finger-actuated valves, a pump, and onboard reagent storage in blister packs, enabling a complete sample-to-eluate workflow encompassing lysis, binding, washing, and elution through manual actuation alone. Performance was benchmarked against both manual benchtop and automated robotic extraction methods using DNA-spiked aqueous samples and human pooled plasma, with the device achieving recovery rates comparable to commercial approaches and even surpassing benchtop controls at lower plasma input volumes. Clinical utility was demonstrated using patient samples positive for cytomegalovirus, monkeypox virus, and chikungunya virus, with quantitative PCR cycle threshold values closely matching those from standard protocols. The authors propose this instrument-free extraction tool as a practical bridge between lateral flow nucleic acid amplification technologies and decentralised molecular diagnostics in resource-limited settings.
items.citation: Musaddaq G, Ehsan L, Yoga Y et al.. Finger-actuated microfluidic device for point-of-care circulating cell-free nucleic acid extraction.. Lab on a chip. 2026

items.title: Molecular point-of-care: technological evolution, clinical applications, and future perspectives
items.citation: Zhang D, Cui X, Zhang R et al.. Molecular point-of-care: technological evolution, clinical applications, and future perspectives. Frontiers in bioengineering and biotechnology. 2026

items.title: Novel near-point of care nucleic acid amplification tests (NPOC NAAT) for TB: addressing readiness at primary health care.
items.citation: Scott LE, Theron G, David A et al.. Novel near-point of care nucleic acid amplification tests (NPOC NAAT) for TB: addressing readiness at primary health care.. IJTLD open. 2026

items.title: Molecular Diagnostics of Infectious Diseases.
items.summary: This review examines the current landscape of molecular diagnostic technologies used to detect and characterize pathogens responsible for infectious diseases. The paper covers two primary approaches: nucleic acid amplification methods, including polymerase chain reaction variants and isothermal amplification techniques, and pathogen characterization through next-generation sequencing. Advances in polymerase chain reaction focus on improving speed, quantification, automation, and point-of-care applicability, while isothermal amplification methods offer advantages for field or bedside testing by eliminating the need for thermal cycling equipment. CRISPR-based detection is highlighted as an emerging complementary tool frequently paired with isothermal amplification, and next-generation sequencing is noted for its capacity to identify novel pathogens, track outbreak transmission, and analyze microbiomes as potential disease biomarkers. The authors conclude that future progress in infectious disease molecular diagnostics will come from integrating these technologies into hybrid platforms that address their individual limitations.
items.citation: Takata M, Chikumi H, Yoshifuji A. Molecular Diagnostics of Infectious Diseases.. Yonago acta medica. 2026

items.title: QMini: A Portable Device for Infectious Disease Testing.
items.summary: The paper studied the development of a portable device for nucleic acid-based infectious disease testing, aiming to address the limitation that conventional testing equipment is too large for field deployment. The researchers built the QMini by simplifying a fluidic module through direct pump-to-chamber connections and shielding an optical detection module from ambient light using a three-dimensional-printed enclosure. They applied the device to detect synthetic nucleic acid sequences from respiratory syncytial virus B, SARS-CoV-2, and influenza A using a bead-based assay with quantum dot barcodes. The QMini successfully detected low copy numbers of each target pathogen and showed limited cross-reactivity against nontarget viral sequences, demonstrating both sensitivity and specificity. The authors conclude that the QMini meaningfully advances the portability of quantum dot barcode-based nucleic acid testing through miniaturization.
items.citation: Mahbub N, Osborne M, Chen H et al.. QMini: A Portable Device for Infectious Disease Testing.. ACS nanoscience Au. 2026

items.title: Gut microbiota dynamics in free-range layer hens during outbreaks of spotty liver disease and fowl cholera—a field study
items.summary: This field study investigated gut microbiota dynamics and flock performance in free-range layer hens during naturally occurring outbreaks of spotty liver disease and fowl cholera, diseases that are difficult to replicate under controlled laboratory conditions. The researchers monitored a commercial layer flock in which one group received a precision biotic consisting of a synthetic glycan product, while a control group did not, with weekly performance measures and microbial community profiling across major gut sections conducted throughout. Birds receiving the precision biotic showed higher egg output but also higher cumulative mortality, alongside differences in intestinal microbial community composition and liver congestion compared to controls. Because the study was unreplicated, the observed differences are interpreted as descriptive associations rather than definitive causal effects. The work highlights the value of on-farm field observations in capturing the complexity of disease dynamics and production pressures that cannot be faithfully reproduced in controlled animal facilities.
items.citation: Friedrich Petranyi, Maria M. Whitton, Edina Lobo et al.. Gut microbiota dynamics in free-range layer hens during outbreaks of spotty liver disease and fowl cholera—a field study. Applied Microbiology and Biotechnology. 2026

items.title: Multi-omics and artificial intelligence for precision drug discovery and potential clinical applications
items.summary: This review examines how the integration of multiomics technologies and artificial intelligence is reshaping precision drug discovery and clinical translation. The authors survey a broad range of multiomics approaches — including genome-wide association studies, transcriptomics, proteomics, and metabolomics — alongside advanced AI methodologies such as deep learning, to characterize how these tools jointly illuminate disease mechanisms at the molecular level. The review covers applications across the drug development pipeline, including target identification, drug repositioning, de novo compound discovery, virtual screening, pharmacokinetic modeling, and safety assessment. Case studies in oncology, neurodegenerative diseases, and cardiovascular conditions are used to illustrate the practical promise of this convergence, while the authors also acknowledge persistent challenges such as harmonizing disparate data streams, ensuring reproducibility, and addressing algorithmic bias. Overall, the paper argues that combining multiomics with AI enables more comprehensive molecular understanding and more precise therapeutic interventions, heralding a new era in bench-to-clinic translational medicine.
items.citation: Yuqing Liu, Kun Zhu, Weijun Peng et al.. Multi-omics and artificial intelligence for precision drug discovery and potential clinical applications. Signal Transduction and Targeted Therapy. 2026

items.title: Regulatory Challenges and Opportunities for Cell‐Derived Extracellular Vesicles in Pharmaceutical Development: A European and Global Perspective
items.summary: The paper examines the regulatory landscape governing cell-derived extracellular vesicles as therapeutic and diagnostic products, with a focus on how their acellular nature creates classification challenges across existing pharmaceutical frameworks. The authors analyze divergent approaches taken by major regulatory jurisdictions, noting that the European framework has recently clarified that minimally modified extracellular vesicles fall outside advanced therapy medicinal product definitions, while other regions apply drug and biologics classifications using their own criteria. This heterogeneity is identified as a source of difficulty for quality assessment, comparability studies, and cross-regional clinical development. The paper argues that extracellular vesicle products should be developed within existing medicinal product frameworks provided regulatory tools are applied consistently, and it maps out operational grey zones—including classification criteria, critical quality attributes, potency strategies, and comparability—that require clarification. Rather than proposing new normative frameworks, the work offers a synthesizing analysis intended to support regulatory dialogue among international agencies and scientific societies to advance these therapies toward safe and reproducible clinical use.
items.citation: Tania Limongi, Paola Milla, Barbara Stella et al.. Regulatory Challenges and Opportunities for Cell‐Derived Extracellular Vesicles in Pharmaceutical Development: A European and Global Perspective. Journal of Extracellular Vesicles. 2026

items.title: Loss-of-function mutation in Omicron variants reduces spike protein expression and attenuates SARS-CoV-2 infection
items.citation: Michelle N. Vu, R. Elias Alvarado, Dorothea R. Morris et al.. Loss-of-function mutation in Omicron variants reduces spike protein expression and attenuates SARS-CoV-2 infection. Nature Communications. 2026

items.title: Smartphone-integrated RPA-CRISPR/Cas12a detection system with microneedle sampling for early point-of-care diagnosis of potato late blight
items.citation: Jinbiao Zhao, Hanbo Xu, Shifang Fei et al.. Smartphone-integrated RPA-CRISPR/Cas12a detection system with microneedle sampling for early point-of-care diagnosis of potato late blight. Biosensors and Bioelectronics. 2026

items.title: The origin, history, and resistance architecture of an invasive urban malaria mosquito in Africa
items.summary: The paper investigated the origins, spread, and insecticide resistance mechanisms of *Anopheles stephensi*, an invasive mosquito species that is an important urban malaria vector now established in Africa. By analyzing hundreds of whole genomes sampled across Africa, the Middle East, and Asia, the researchers reconstructed the invasion history of this species. They found that the mosquito was first introduced from South Asia, establishing a bridgehead population in Djibouti that subsequently gave rise to distinct invasion fronts in Sudan, Ethiopia and Kenya, and Yemen, with the rates and routes of spread shaped by local landscape features. Insecticide resistance was found to be driven primarily by metabolic detoxification genes, with the key resistance variants and gene copy-number amplifications having been brought in from South Asia rather than arising independently in Africa. The study also provides a genomic resource intended to support ongoing surveillance of the mosquito's spread and resistance evolution to inform control efforts.
items.citation: Tristan P. W. Dennis, Jihad Eltaher Sulieman, Mujahid Nouredayem et al.. The origin, history, and resistance architecture of an invasive urban malaria mosquito in Africa. Science. 2026

items.title: Is Neutrino Disappearance Sensitive to T-Violation for Asymmetric Matter Profiles ?
items.summary: This paper reexamines the widely held claim that T violation is absent in neutrino disappearance channels, arguing that this conclusion is not universally valid. The authors demonstrate that the claim holds only for symmetric matter profiles or when the Jarlskog invariant vanishes, and that muon and tau neutrino survival probabilities can carry a genuine T-asymmetric term dependent on the sine of the CP-violating phase when matter profiles are asymmetric. They clarify the distinction between proper and improper tests of T, CP, and CPT symmetry for arbitrary matter profiles, showing that the standard argument relies on an improper T test that amounts to a mathematical identity rather than a physical result. Using a two-layer constant-density toy model, they find that T violation is maximized when one layer is near the solar resonance and the other near the atmospheric resonance. The paper further assesses whether the matter asymmetry encountered by experiments such as DUNE and Hyper-Kamiokande is sufficient to make this effect observable in muon neutrino survival probability, and discusses future experimental scenarios that could probe T and CP violation through this channel.
items.citation: Gabriela Barenboim, Stephen J. Parke, Alberto Sánchez Vargas. Is Neutrino Disappearance Sensitive to T-Violation for Asymmetric Matter Profiles ?. arXiv. 2026

items.title: Your Camera Can Hear You: Side-Channel Acoustic Eavesdropping via Android Camera2 Metadata
items.summary: This paper investigates a novel side-channel attack that exploits Android's Camera2 subsystem to perform acoustic eavesdropping without requiring microphone permissions. The researchers discovered that camera hardware abstraction layer stabilization pipelines capture high-rate gyroscope measurements and export them through vendor metadata, bypassing Android's motion sensor privacy defenses entirely—including the microphone and camera privacy toggles introduced in Android 12. Testing across a broad range of smartphones from multiple vendors, they found that a substantial proportion expose gyroscope data at sampling rates far exceeding the system's intended caps, with some flagship devices streaming at nearly double the allowed ceiling even when privacy switches are engaged. To exploit this channel without device-specific training data, the authors developed Source-to-Leakage Learning, a physics-constrained simulation framework that decouples speech content from a phone's mechanical resonance characteristics, enabling a universal speech recognizer trained entirely on synthetic data. Their resulting system, CamEar, substantially outperforms prior approaches on unseen devices, demonstrating that simulated training can generalize across hardware in ways that real-data fine-tuning cannot.
items.citation: Guangyuan Ji, Wenjing Wang, Bingsheng Zhang. Your Camera Can Hear You: Side-Channel Acoustic Eavesdropping via Android Camera2 Metadata. arXiv. 2026

items.title: Receptor Abundance Alone Underpredicts Red Blood Cell Adhesion in Gaucher Disease
items.summary: This paper investigated why red blood cells in Gaucher disease adhere abnormally to vessel walls, asking whether the known increase in Lutheran/basal cell adhesion molecule receptor abundance is sufficient to explain the elevated adhesion. The researchers developed a computational model simulating stochastic receptor-ligand bond formation, calibrated it using control donor data, and then applied it to predict adhesion in Gaucher disease based on the measured receptor increase. The model systematically underpredicted observed adhesion on both laminin and endothelium, and closing this gap required assuming a much larger increase in binding-competent receptors than the total receptor count suggests, consistent with a substantially greater rise in phosphorylated, active receptors. The findings indicate that receptor activation state rather than total receptor abundance governs adhesion, a conclusion further supported by the model's ability to predict reduced adhesion under hydroxyurea treatment in sickle cell disease when active receptor counts are used. Additionally, membrane stiffening was found not to rescue adhesion predictions at high shear stress but instead may promote cell retention at splenic slits, suggesting distinct mechanical consequences for disease-related membrane changes.
items.citation: Zhaojie Chai, Pierre A. Buffet, Melanie Franco et al.. Receptor Abundance Alone Underpredicts Red Blood Cell Adhesion in Gaucher Disease. arXiv. 2026

items.title: Ranking-Preserving Coreset Selection for Efficient Evolutionary Hyperparameter Optimization
items.summary: This paper addresses the computational burden of hyperparameter optimization on large datasets by proposing a framework that selects a compact subset of training data, called a ranking-preserving coreset, which faithfully reproduces the relative performance ordering of hyperparameter configurations seen on the full dataset. The coreset selection itself is framed as an evolutionary optimization problem that maximizes the Spearman rank correlation between full-data and subset-based configuration rankings while simultaneously penalizing larger subset sizes. The resulting coreset is then used as a drop-in replacement for the full dataset during hyperparameter search with three evolutionary algorithms spanning genetic and swarm-based approaches. Experiments across tabular, text, and image benchmark datasets demonstrate that the method substantially reduces the time spent in the hyperparameter optimization stage while preserving test accuracy comparable to full-data optimization, with the one-time coreset construction cost amortizable over multiple optimization runs. Notably, the ranking preservation property generalizes to configurations not seen during coreset construction, outperforming random subsampling of equal size on the majority of datasets tested.
items.citation: Mamoona Tasadduq, Maryam Bashir. Ranking-Preserving Coreset Selection for Efficient Evolutionary Hyperparameter Optimization. arXiv. 2026

items.title: Recovering buoyancy-glitch parameters in low-luminosity red giants from global stellar properties with machine learning
items.summary: This paper investigated whether the properties of buoyancy glitches in low-luminosity red giants — features that encode localized information about stellar interior structure near the base of the convective envelope — can be recovered from global stellar observables rather than through computationally expensive dedicated seismic modelling. The researchers trained gradient-boosted tree machine learning models on a large grid of synthetic stellar models, using global properties to predict the amplitude, location, and width of buoyancy glitches derived from fits to the local buoyancy frequency profile. The glitch location and width were recovered with high accuracy, while the glitch amplitude showed moderate overall recoverability that degraded in a specific range of large frequency separations where the glitch lies in a structurally complex transition region between the convective envelope and the gravity-mode cavity. Interpretability analysis revealed that the effective temperature and the frequency of maximum oscillation power dominate predictions across all three parameters, suggesting the models primarily exploit evolutionary state information. The authors conclude that global stellar properties offer a viable route to estimating buoyancy-glitch parameters at scale, which could help prioritize which stars in large surveys warrant the more intensive analysis of mixed-mode inversions.
items.citation: Jiang Chen. Recovering buoyancy-glitch parameters in low-luminosity red giants from global stellar properties with machine learning. arXiv. 2026

items.title: One partition function call to rule them all: Efficiently computing the equilibrium landscape of multiple nucleic acid strands
items.summary: This paper addresses the computational problem of analyzing the thermodynamic behavior of multiple interacting nucleic acid strands under the nearest-neighbor model, where the partition function sums Boltzmann-weighted free energies over an exponentially large set of secondary structures. The authors introduce a concept called a "magnifiable" partition function algorithm, which encodes the full energy landscape in a way that allows diverse prediction problems to be solved efficiently from a single algorithmic framework. Their algorithm matches the time and space complexity of the previously known non-magnifiable partition function approach while extending its utility dramatically. Through this unified framework, they achieve improvements to minimum free energy computation for multiple strands, as well as the first polynomial-time algorithms for the multi-stranded density of states problem, enumeration of all occupied energy levels, and several other energy landscape and counting problems. The work demonstrates that a single general algorithmic construction can replace a collection of previously distinct techniques while simultaneously improving or matching their computational bounds.
items.citation: Ahmed Shalaby, Damien Woods. One partition function call to rule them all: Efficiently computing the equilibrium landscape of multiple nucleic acid strands. arXiv. 2026

items.title: Diagnostic performance of antigen-based rapid test kits for six respiratory viruses in children: comparison with a multiplex PCR panel and correlation with viral load.
items.summary: This study examined how well antigen-based rapid tests perform for diagnosing six common respiratory viruses in children, and specifically how their sensitivity relates to viral load. Using a prospective paired-specimen design, nasopharyngeal swabs from children with respiratory tract infections were tested in parallel with rapid antigen kits and a multiplex PCR panel, with positive specimens further analyzed by quantitative real-time PCR to quantify viral burden. Across all six viral targets — SARS-CoV-2, influenza A, influenza B, adenovirus, human metapneumovirus, and respiratory syncytial virus — specificity exceeded ninety-nine percent, while sensitivity varied considerably by pathogen and was strongly dependent on viral load. At high viral loads, antigen test sensitivity approached ninety to one hundred percent regardless of the target virus, whereas at low viral loads it fell below fifty percent. The authors conclude that rapid antigen tests reliably identify children carrying the highest viral burdens, supporting their clinical utility for detecting acute, symptomatic infection most likely to require immediate management.
items.citation: Kitagawa D, Di Lorenzo A, Okamura T et al.. Diagnostic performance of antigen-based rapid test kits for six respiratory viruses in children: comparison with a multiplex PCR panel and correlation with viral load.. Journal of clinical microbiology. 2026

items.title: Diagnostic yield of reflex multiplex PCR after a negative rapid antigen test in children hospitalized with presumed viral acute respiratory tract infection: a prospective cohort study.
items.summary: The study investigated whether adding reflex multiplex PCR testing after a negative rapid antigen test improves viral detection in children hospitalized with presumed viral acute respiratory infections. In a prospective single-center cohort, children first underwent a five-target rapid antigen test, and those who tested negative could then receive a broader multiplex PCR panel at physician discretion. The reflex PCR substantially increased diagnostic yield, with the large majority of antigen-negative children who received it testing positive for a respiratory virus, most commonly rhinovirus/enterovirus, which was not covered by the antigen panel. These results demonstrate that a negative rapid antigen test cannot reliably exclude a viral cause of illness, and that broader molecular testing meaningfully expands pathogen identification across different viruses and age groups. Despite high rates of viral detection overall, antibiotic use remained frequent and was not significantly associated with viral detection status, though the appropriateness of antibiotic prescribing could not be fully assessed without systematic bacterial testing.
items.citation: Bedir AZ, Saf C, Yörük MA. Diagnostic yield of reflex multiplex PCR after a negative rapid antigen test in children hospitalized with presumed viral acute respiratory tract infection: a prospective cohort study.. Irish journal of medical science. 2026

items.title: Respiratory virus prevalence among healthcare university students in Ecuador: a multicenter cross-sectional study.
items.summary: This cross-sectional study investigated the prevalence of respiratory viruses among healthcare university students across three cities in Ecuador, a population considered at elevated risk due to social contact and clinical exposure. Researchers collected nasopharyngeal samples from several hundred students and tested them on-site using rapid antigen tests capable of detecting influenza A, influenza B, respiratory syncytial virus, and adenovirus. The overall prevalence of respiratory virus detection was low, with influenza A and RSV being the most frequently identified pathogens and a small number of coinfections also observed. Notably, more than half of the positive students were asymptomatic at the time of testing, and a significant association was found between symptom presence and viral detection. The authors conclude that respiratory viruses likely circulate undetected in university settings and that the true prevalence is probably underestimated given the limited sensitivity of rapid antigen tests, calling for follow-up studies using molecular methods with larger samples.
items.citation: Bruno A, de Mora D, Olmedo M et al.. Respiratory virus prevalence among healthcare university students in Ecuador: a multicenter cross-sectional study.. Frontiers in public health. 2026

items.title: Diagnostic Accuracy of the RapidFor™ RSV/ADV Rapid Test Kit Compared with PCR for the Detection of Respiratory Syncytial Virus and Adenovirus in Nasopharyngeal Swab Samples
items.summary: This study evaluated the diagnostic performance of a point-of-care rapid antigen test for respiratory syncytial virus and adenovirus against multiplex real-time PCR as the reference standard in children presenting to a pediatric emergency department with acute respiratory symptoms. A prospective design was used in which paired nasopharyngeal swabs were collected from pediatric patients, with one processed by the rapid kit immediately at bedside and the other by PCR. The rapid test demonstrated very high sensitivity, specificity, and predictive values for both pathogens, with excellent agreement with PCR results. Age-related patterns of infection were observed, with RSV predominating in infants and adenovirus more common in school-aged children, and distinct clinical predictors were identified for each pathogen. The authors conclude that this dual rapid test offers clinically useful accuracy and may support timely decision-making in pediatric emergency settings where PCR is not immediately available.
items.citation: Ates B, Kacar A, Kok S et al.. Diagnostic Accuracy of the RapidFor™ RSV/ADV Rapid Test Kit Compared with PCR for the Detection of Respiratory Syncytial Virus and Adenovirus in Nasopharyngeal Swab Samples. 2026
